formulaCard.formula: $$\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n},\qquad \mu = \frac{\sum x}{N}$$ $$\text{Median} = \begin{cases} \text{middle ordered value}, & n \text{ odd} \\ \frac{x_{(n/2)} + x_{(n/2+1)}}{2}, & n \text{ even} \end{cases}$$ $$\text{Mode} = \text{most frequent value(s)}$$

formulaCard.title: Definitions

explanation: A [[kw:measure of central tendency]] is a single value that represents a typical, central entry of a data set.
The [[kw:mean]] (arithmetic average) is the sum of all data entries divided by the number of entries.
Population mean: $ \mu = \frac{\sum x}{N} $, sample mean: $ \bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n} $.
The [[kw:median]] is the middle value when the data are ordered. For odd $ n $, it's the center entry; for even $ n $, it's the average of the two center entries.
The [[kw:mode]] is the data entry that occurs with the greatest frequency. A data set can be unimodal, bimodal, multimodal, or have no mode.
The mean uses every value, the median is resistant to outliers, and the mode works for qualitative data as well.

discoveryHook.scenario: Your course grade is a weighted mean: tests 50%, midterm 15%, final 20%, etc. Or you're given a frequency distribution of internet session times — you don't have the original data, only class midpoints. Both situations require a special way to find the mean: weighting each value.

explanation: A [[kw:weighted mean]] is the mean of a data set whose entries have different degrees of importance (weights).
Weighted mean formula: $ \bar{x} = \frac{\sum (x \cdot w)}{\sum w} $, where $ w $ is the weight of each value $ x $.
When data are grouped into a frequency distribution, we approximate the mean by treating each class midpoint $ x $ as representative of that class, weighted by its frequency $ f $.
Mean of grouped data (sample): $ \bar{x} = \frac{\sum (x \cdot f)}{n} $, where $ n = \sum f $.

explanation: A distribution is [[kw:symmetric]] if a vertical line divides it into mirror images. In a symmetric unimodal distribution, the mean, median, and mode are equal.
A [[kw:uniform]] (rectangular) distribution has all classes with approximately equal frequencies. It is also symmetric.
A distribution is [[kw:skewed right]] (positively skewed) if the tail extends to the right. Here, $ \text{mean} > \text{median} > \text{mode} $ (usually).
A distribution is [[kw:skewed left]] (negatively skewed) if the tail extends to the left. Here, $ \text{mean} < \text{median} < \text{mode} $ (usually).
The mean is pulled in the direction of the skew. The median is more resistant.

discoveryHook.scenario: The shape of a data distribution tells a story: whether the data are balanced, flat, or pulled toward one end. And the shape determines the relationship among the mean, median, and mode — the three musketeers of central tendency.

teacherCues: Sketch a symmetric bell‑shaped curve, a uniform rectangle, a right‑skewed tail, and a left‑skewed tail. Ask students which one fits test scores that are mostly high but a few failed.

The mean and median will be close together, both near the center.

explanation: An [[kw:outlier]] is a data entry far removed from the rest of the data.
Outliers can dramatically affect the [[imp:mean]] but usually have little effect on the [[imp:median]] or [[imp:mode]].
When outliers are present, the median often provides a better measure of central tendency than the mean.
To decide which measure best represents the data: examine the shape, identify any outliers, and choose the measure that stays closest to the bulk of the data.

discoveryHook.scenario: A small class of 20‑somethings has one 65‑year‑old student. If you report the mean age, it might look like the class is much older than it really is. The median stays firmly in the 20s, but the mean jumps. This is why it's crucial to compare measures and check for outliers.

confusionCorner.title: Outliers Aren't Always 'Wrong'
confusionCorner.body: An outlier may be a valid data point that carries important information. Don't automatically delete it; investigate whether it's a measurement error or a genuine extreme. [[imp:Report measures with and without the outlier to give a complete picture.]]

blocks.title: Comparing Measures and the Effect of Outliers

discoveryHook.scenario: Given any data set, the blueprint guides you: understand its shape and whether it has outliers, solve by selecting the right measure and computing it, and conclude by stating what the measure tells you about the data. A structured approach prevents you from blindly averaging and misrepresenting the data.

explanation: Blueprint: [[imp:Understand → Solve → Conclude]].
1. [[kw:Understand]]: Examine the data. Is it quantitative? Check the shape (symmetric, skewed, uniform) and look for outliers (using a stem‑and‑leaf plot, dot plot, or sorted list).

2. [[kw:Solve]]: Choose the measure. If symmetric with no outliers, the mean is a good choice. If skewed or with outliers, prefer the median. If the most frequent value is of interest, also report the mode. For qualitative data, the mode is the only option. Compute using the appropriate formula (mean, weighted mean, grouped mean).
3. [[kw:Conclude]]: Report the value(s) in context, noting any cautions (e.g., 'The mean is $23.8 but is inflated by an outlier; the median of $21.5 better represents the typical age').

title: Measures of Central Tendency
presenterNotes: Block 1: Emphasize the formulas and the difference between population mean (μ) and sample mean (x̄). The flight prices example is memorable because it shows all three measures on the same data.
Block 2: The weighted mean is intuitive for grades. The grouped mean connects back to frequency distributions from Section 2.1 — revisit midpoints.
Block 3: Use drawings to make the shapes stick. The mean-median-mode relationship is a key concept that students often confuse. The table should help.
Block 4: The class age data with the 65-year-old outlier is a powerful demonstration. Remove the outlier and show the shift. Drive home that median is resistant.
Block 5: This blueprint ties everything together. Emphasize that you should always examine the shape and check for outliers before choosing a measure.
